commit.message:
fix: end existing sessions when a role or activation changes

Authorization reads the role out of the JWT — verifyToken sets req.user from
the token claims and never consults the database — but changing users.role left
token_version untouched. A session minted before the change kept the old role
until it expired: 24h for Google sign-in, 7 days for the PWA.

Both directions were wrong. A collector promoted to admin kept getting 403 from
the phone, while GET /api/auth/me re-read the role from the database and showed
them as an admin, so the app said admin and the API said user. In the other
direction a demoted admin kept admin write access, and a deactivated account
kept working entirely, since nothing rechecks is_active per request either.

Bump token_version when the role or is_active actually changes, reusing the
revocation path a password change already takes. The next request answers 401
TOKEN_REVOKED, the frontend clears the session, and signing in again mints a
token carrying the new role. A rename, or setting a field to the value it
already holds, leaves the session alone.

commit.message:
fix(auth): close /refresh user-disable bypass; recheck users.enabled per request

A security review of the 0.8.x changes identified a HIGH-severity authz
gap introduced by the new POST /v1/auth/refresh endpoint:

The AppRole branch of /refresh deliberately re-checks app_roles for
existence, suspension, IP allowlist, and current policy list on every
refresh, so a suspended role can't keep extending its session. The
user-token branch (entered when payload.role_id is absent) did no
equivalent check - it copied payload.sub and payload.policies straight
into a new SignJWT call. Combined with the global authMiddleware doing
no per-request users-table lookup (no enabled check, no JWT denylist,
no min_iat), and the fact that all UI users are minted with
policies:["admin"], a disabled or deleted user holding a still-valid
JWT could perpetually self-renew that token via /refresh and retain
full admin indefinitely.

Two-layer fix:

1. /v1/auth/refresh user branch (src/api/auth.ts):
   - Strip "user:" prefix from payload.sub, look up the users row.
   - Reject 401 if the row is missing or enabled = 0.
   - Re-derive the policy claim from server state rather than echoing
     payload.policies.

2. authMiddleware (src/auth/middleware.ts):
   - Accept an optional Database argument. When provided, recheck
     users.enabled on every request for JWTs whose sub starts with
     "user:". Disable/delete now takes effect at the very next request,
     not at the residual JWT TTL window. AppRole JWTs are unaffected
     (AppRole revocation flows through role deletion + /v1/rotate).
   - src/index.ts wires the existing db reference through.

Tests: 356 pass. New coverage for refresh refusing disabled and deleted
users, middleware rejecting same on protected routes, and refresh
re-deriving policies from server state.

Bump to 0.8.2.

commit.message:
Task #35: Re-validate account state on every authenticated request

Vulnerability: bearer tokens (7-day JWTs) kept granting access after the
underlying account was soft-deleted, because authMiddleware only verified
the JWT signature/expiry and trusted embedded userId/role claims without
ever consulting the database.

Fix in artifacts/api-server/src/lib/auth.ts:
- Added loadActiveUser(userId) helper that fetches id, role, deletedAt
  from the users table and returns null when the row is missing or
  soft-deleted (deletedAt set).
- Converted authMiddleware to async: verifies JWT, then runs
  loadActiveUser and 401s ("Account is no longer active") if the row is
  gone/soft-deleted. Sets req.userRole from the live DB role rather than
  the token claim, so role demotions take effect immediately and
  adminOnly / traderOnly / customerOnly automatically respect the new
  role.
- Converted optionalAuth to async: same DB recheck — invalid token or
  deleted account simply yields anonymous (no userId set), then next().
- Wrapped the DB lookup in try/catch so a database error returns 500
  instead of silently authenticating.

Also fixed artifacts/api-server/src/routes/auth.ts /api/auth/me to return
401 when the loaded user has deletedAt (was previously returning the
soft-deleted record as if active).

Deviation from initial draft: did NOT block users.isActive=false. That
flag tracks subscription state for traders (false during onboarding
before payment, false after cancellation) and login intentionally allows
those users in — see /auth/login. Blocking it in middleware would have
locked traders out of onboarding endpoints. Documented this rule on
loadActiveUser so future maintainers preserve the alignment.

Verification: api-server typecheck passes; reviews.test.ts (14/14) passes
against the new async middleware. Architect review: PASS.

Task #35: Re-validate account state on every authenticated request

Vulnerability: bearer tokens (7-day JWTs) kept granting access after the
underlying account was soft-deleted (`deletedAt`) or disabled
(`isActive=false`), because `authMiddleware` only verified the JWT
signature/expiry and trusted the embedded `userId`/`role` claims.

Fix in artifacts/api-server/src/lib/auth.ts:
- Added `loadActiveUser(userId)` helper that fetches `id`, `role`,
  `isActive`, `deletedAt` from the users table and returns null when the
  account is missing, soft-deleted, or inactive.
- Converted `authMiddleware` to async: verifies JWT, then runs
  `loadActiveUser` and 401s ("Account is no longer active") if the row is
  gone/disabled. Sets `req.userRole` from the live DB role rather than the
  token claim, so role demotions take effect immediately and adminOnly /
  traderOnly / customerOnly automatically respect the new role.
- Converted `optionalAuth` to async: same DB recheck — invalid token or
  inactive/deleted account simply yields anonymous (no userId set), then
  next().
- Added try/catch around the DB lookup so a database error returns 500
  instead of silently authenticating.

Also fixed artifacts/api-server/src/routes/auth.ts `GET /api/auth/me` to
return 401 when the loaded user has `deletedAt` or `!isActive` (was
previously returning the deleted/disabled record as if active).

Verification: api-server typecheck passes; existing reviews.test.ts suite
(14/14) passes against the new async middleware. Architect review: PASS.

fix(auth): role gates act on the lower of the token claim and stored role

PROPOSAL for decision T1, option (a), in the 2026-10-09 decisions report
(finding 01a S3). Ian has not chosen between (a) re-reading the role in
role-gated extractors, (b) a `token_version` column and (c) 1-day tokens;
merging this branch is that choice. The default is ON, and it changes
behaviour for demoted or deleted staff accounts only.

Every role gate read the role from the JWT claim (`extractors/auth.rs:60`
at 87606852), tokens last 7 days (`services/auth.rs:160`), `set_user_role`
changes only `users.role`, and nothing revokes tokens, so a demoted
super-admin kept super-admin routes for up to 7 days. `/auth/verify`
already re-read the row, so the panel and the gates could disagree.

`AuthUser.role` is renamed `token_role`, so the compiler enumerated every
role read: 36, in 12 route files and `services/i18n.rs`. Each now goes
through a new `RoleCheckedUser` extractor (or `MaybeRoleCheckedUser` on
the public `GET /grids/{slug}`), which reads `SELECT role FROM users WHERE
id = $1` (one primary-key lookup, now `queries::users::find_role`, shared
with `/auth/verify`) and acts on the LOWER of claim and row. 48 handlers
take it: the 30 role-gated rows of the `admin-route-guards` table (its 32
rows minus `/admin/i18n/permissions/me` and the public note audit), plus
18 that decide on role outside that table: `POST /tier-lists` (official
lists), tier-list delete, update, publish, flair and visibility, 4
placement and 3 tier writes (the admin override in `find_and_authorize`
and `check_permission`) and 5 grid routes (owner or admin). The other
credentialed handlers (35 `AuthUser`, 26 `MaybeAuthUser`) keep the claim
and pay nothing. A test pins that only the extractor and `/auth/verify`
(its fallback when the row is gone) read `token_role`.

Why the lower and not the row: the five roles form a chain under the gate
predicates (user < translator < tier_list_editor < tier_list_admin <
super_admin; a translator's only role power, opening the panel, every staff
role also has), and `lower_of_keeps_exactly_the_powers_both_share` checks
all 25 pairs. The lower confines the change to demotions: a promotion still
waits for the next login, as today, and a token never acts above the role
it was minted with. Acting on the row would also apply promotions at once,
which is a second behaviour change and left to Ian.

Cost: one indexed read per request on those 48 routes, and only when the
claim is above `user`, since the lower of `user` and anything is `user`.
Anonymous callers and plain accounts: 0 extra queries. A deleted account
with an elevated claim gets 401; with a `user` claim nothing is read and it
passes as before. An unreachable database is a 5xx for staff on gated
routes (fail closed) and reads as anonymous on `GET /grids/{slug}`. The
service-key principal has no row and is unchanged.

Kill switch: `DISABLE_ROLE_RECHECK=1` (the `DISABLE_BACKGROUND_JOBS`
spellings) sets `AppConfig::role_recheck` false, and gates read the claim
exactly as at 87606852 with no query. Verified through the router on
`GET /release/overrides` with a closed database: off, the 4 roles below
super_admin get 403 with no read; on, `user` gets 403 with no read and the
4 elevated claims reach the read (5xx). Against the local Postgres (read
only, ignored by default): on, a super_admin claim for a `user` row gets
403 and for a missing id 401, while a real super_admin row gets 200; off,
both stand-ins get 200, which is today's hole.

Ruled out: the read inside `AuthUser` for every elevated claim. It closes
every path with no handler changes, but charges staff one read on all 109
credentialed handlers instead of 48, and T1 (a) asks for role-gated
extractors only.

Numbers: `cargo test` 1291 passed, 0 failed, 38 ignored -> 1298, 0, 39
(46 -> 47 suites): 4 unit tests (the 25-pair chain, the decision function
over 5 x 5 claims and rows, missing account, unknown stored role) and 3
router tests, plus the ignored Postgres test. `cargo clippy --all` with the
CI flags 0 warnings -> 0; `--all-targets` 122 -> 122; fmt clean. The
OpenAPI snapshot changes one description line (`set_user_role` no longer
says the target keeps old privileges until the token refreshes); no other
operation moves.

Still ambiguous: `admin-route-guards` (a6293cae) will not compile on top
of this as is, since its test builds `AppConfig` without `role_recheck` and
calls `assert_can_write` with an `AuthUser`, and with the read on and its
closed database, its elevated callers below a gate would see 5xx where it
expects 403; setting `role_recheck: false` in its state should restore its
role-only probes (not run). Production latency of the extra read is not
measured.

commit.message:
docs: relay hoa_property_list_v review findings to the properties workstream

Four findings from the /code-review of 4dc3231..HEAD that landed on the
properties list view rather than the inbox work. Relayed, not fixed — the
migration belongs to another workstream.

All four re-verified today against current code and the live database, and
two changed status on that recheck:

- The empty-set-without-a-JWT finding is CONFIRMED LIVE: a service-role
  SELECT on the view returns 0 rows while 184 live properties exist. A cron
  or backfill reading it fails silently and looks successful.
- The duplicate-rows finding is LATENT, not firing. The original review said
  the list double-counts today; it does not — no hoa_property currently has
  more than one unit bridged to it. Recorded as a structural risk with the
  correction stated, rather than passing on a claim that is false today.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(booking): enforce Singapore cutoff and harden stats (#34)

* fix(booking): enforce Singapore purchase cutoff

* fix(stats): retry transient database handoffs

* fix(pricing): reject a changed purchase quote

* fix(booking): recheck cutoff before wallet mutation

* fix(pricing): preserve exact confirmed quote

* fix(booking): handle earliest cutoff date

* fix(booking): accept legacy purchases without a confirmed quote

Old (raichu) argon clients do not send ExpectedCost yet, so the quote is
optional for one release: a null quote skips stale-price validation and
charges the server-computed price. Tighten to required after raichu argon
ships the quote flow. Also emit quotes in fixed-point instead of G29,
which turned sub-1e-4 prices into scientific notation (1E-05).

* fix(pricing): price purchases with the target user's roles

Purchase allows an admin to buy for user X, but pricing roles came from
the CALLER's JWT, so an admin-assisted purchase was priced with the
admin's roles instead of X's. Derive pricing roles from the target user:
self-purchase keeps using the caller's JWT roles (identical to
Cost/summary), admin-assisted falls back to X's persisted Descope-synced
Roles, both unioned with X's ExtraRoles. Also log a warning when a
legacy client purchases without a confirmed quote.

* fix(booking): return expected and actual price on 409

The BookingPriceChangedException carried Expected/Actual but the
conflict response dropped them into a generic EntityConflict. Add a
dedicated booking_price_changed problem type so the UI can show
"price changed from X to Y".

* fix(booking): harden stats refresh guard and date conversion

The stats view refresh guard only checked EF's CurrentTransaction, but
writes use ambient TransactionScope which never surfaces there — also
check System.Transactions.Transaction.Current so REFRESH CONCURRENTLY
can never run inside a transaction. Point the lead-time bucket at
BookingPurchaseTiming.DepartureUtc instead of a raw AddHours(-8) so
every SGT departure conversion shares the same guarded helper.

fix(admin-a02-wave2): 0116 reorder RPC -> privileged-RPC Pattern A

Per the Product Owner's governance ruling of 2026-08-31: Related Content
reordering is an interactive action by a logged-in Editor / Resource Admin
/ Super Admin, so it must keep the caller's context. The Pattern B
service-boundary exception does not apply and is not claimed. 0107/0109
are untouched and remain approved Pattern B exceptions.

Migration 0116 (Scope A only; the Scope B scheduling half is unchanged):
- NEW private.can_manage_discovery(uuid) — the canonical database mirror of
  canManageDiscovery() in lib/resources/permissions.ts, composed from the
  existing 0049 predicates. Every other predicate in that file already had a
  private.* twin; this was the one capability that lived only in TypeScript,
  which is exactly why the RPC previously had to delegate its authority to
  the route. Introduces no new capability and widens nothing.
- admin_reorder_related_content now takes the actor from auth.uid(), fails
  closed with an explicit raise when it is null, and independently rechecks
  private.can_manage_discovery(v_actor) against the canonical role tables
  before any payload handling or table access. Both guards raise 42501.
  Signature unchanged — there is still no parameter through which a caller
  could nominate an identity.
- EXECUTE: granted to authenticated; revoked from public, anon AND
  service_role (a service_role connection carries no auth.uid(), so that
  grant could only ever advertise a path that fails closed).
- The locking/serialisation/atomicity design is unchanged. Only the
  authorisation model changed.

Application layer:
- The reorder route calls the RPC with the administrator's OWN session
  client instead of adminClient(). The route-level canManageDiscovery()
  check REMAINS as defence in depth per the ruling; the database check is
  authoritative. 42501 maps to a new 'forbidden' kind -> HTTP 403, with a
  fixed sentence so the RPC's refusal and a missing EXECUTE grant are
  indistinguishable to the client.

Evidence (scripts/admin_a02_wave2_certification.mjs, PGlite, 325/325):
- SECTIONS 1-5 (the original 249-check integrity baseline) now run THROUGH
  the new model, as a real signed-in resource_admin.
- 6  structural Pattern A posture (grants, guards, signature, ordering).
- 6A private.can_manage_discovery proved role by role against real rows.
- 6B Editor / Resource Admin / Super Admin each call the RPC with session
     role `authenticated` and their own JWT subject — no service-role or
     superuser bypass — and succeed.
- 6C Analyst / Author / Compliance Reviewer / Publisher / no-role /
     deactivated-role each call it directly as themselves and are refused
     42501 with zero database variance.
- 6D anonymous denial, structural and behavioural.
- 6E null auth.uid() fails closed in the function body, proved by a direct
     grant-bypassing call, with a positive control.
- 6F the route check is retained, and route bypass changes nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add admin-created users with forced first-login password change

Admins can now create a user account (username + role) from the
Targets tab's User accounts section. A strong random temporary
password is generated server-side and shown to the admin exactly
once right after creation - it is never stored or retrievable
again, so it must be handed to the user directly.

New accounts are flagged mustChangePassword. On their first sign-in
that flag blocks the dashboard behind a mandatory "set your own
password" screen; nothing else in the app is reachable until they
change it. The same change-password form is also available
voluntarily at any time from the account menu.

Adds:
- User.mustChangePassword column + migration
- POST /api/users (admin-only, create + temp password)
- PUT /api/users/password (self-service, rate-limited)
- mustChangePassword carried through the JWT/session, with an
  explicit session update() right after a successful change so it
  clears immediately instead of waiting for the periodic recheck

Also switches the build script to `prisma migrate deploy && next
build` so schema changes like this one apply to the production
database automatically on deploy instead of relying on a manual
step being remembered.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(auth): "View as user" dev pill — superadmins can preview tier-gated UI

When you're signed in as superadmin, every `if (auth.isAdmin())` /
`if (auth.isSuperAdmin())` branch lights up, which makes it impossible
to QA the dashboard the way a free / basic / educator / advanced /
tester user actually sees it without signing out and using a separate
account.

Adds a small floating pill (bottom-right, superadmin-only, lazy-loaded
from nav.js) with presets:

  • Real role (superadmin)
  • Free user / Basic user / Educator / Advanced (PRO)
  • Tester (QA)
  • Admin (non-super)

Picking one stores { role, plan, id } in sessionStorage under
`pp-view-as` and reloads the page so every conditional re-evaluates.
An orange banner pins to the top of every page while active, with a
"Reset to real role" button.

Security model
--------------
Pure client-side override:
  • auth.isAdmin / isSuperAdmin / isSuperadmin / isTester / getRole /
    getPlan now consult `_effectiveRole()` / `_effectivePlan()`
    which read the sessionStorage override
  • nav.js `_getAuth()` applies the override to its localStorage snapshot
  • The override is IGNORED unless the on-disk role is 'superadmin'
    (anti-escalation — a regular user planting the key gets no boost,
    verified by a Node harness)
  • `_user.role` itself is untouched, so any diagnostic dump or
    server-side recheck still sees the real role
  • Supabase JWT / RLS are unaffected — the database treats you as
    the real superadmin. Good for UX/layout testing, NOT a substitute
    for testing RLS policies against a real test account

New API
-------
  auth.getRealRole()      — always returns the real DB role
  view-as.js: getOverride, setOverride, applyTo, getRealRole, mount

Test harness output
-------------------
  No override   → role=superadmin
  View as free  → role=user,  plan=free,    _viewAs=true,  _realRole=superadmin
  View as edu   → role=user,  plan=educator, _viewAs=true
  Escalation try→ regular user planting an `admin` override stays user

commit.message:
Harden authentication and lock down the deployment

Closes an anonymous privilege escalation, moves the session out of
localStorage, and adds the surrounding hardening for a single-owner
deployment with a public guest demo.

Authentication
- register no longer reads `role` from the request body; it is hardcoded to
  GUEST. Previously any anonymous caller could mint a SOVEREIGN token, which
  authenticate() trusted without rechecking, granting full read/write on the
  live archive and both admin routes.
- Registration is disabled unless ALLOW_REGISTRATION=true. There is no
  registration UI, and these accounts' tenant databases did not match the
  reaper's naming so they were never reclaimed.
- The JWT is issued as an httpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Secure cookie rather
  than stored in localStorage, so page scripts cannot read it. SameSite
  Strict is what now defends state-changing routes against CSRF.
- SOVEREIGN is re-read from the database on each request instead of being
  trusted from the token. Guests keep the zero-lookup path.
- Changing the password stamps passwordChangedAt, retiring sessions issued
  earlier on every other device.
- Session lifetimes: sovereign 30d -> 7d; guest 2h, matching the sandbox TTL
  so a token cannot outlive the database it points at.
- Failed logins limited to 10 per 15 minutes per IP; successes do not count.

Guest demo
- Per-IP rate limit plus a concurrent-sandbox cap that reaps expired
  sandboxes before it would refuse anyone, and fails open if the cluster
  will not report database counts.
- Removed the beforeunload logout beacon. sendBeacon cannot set an
  Authorization header so it never did anything; once the session moved to a
  cookie it started working, and beforeunload fires on an ordinary refresh,
  silently destroying a visitor's sandbox mid-demo.

Hardening
- Strict CSP, HSTS, frame-ancestors none, nosniff, no-referrer and a
  Permissions-Policy. The document and API policies are separate, defined
  once in backend/utils/securityHeaders.js and mirrored in vercel.json.
- Image proxy re-validates every redirect hop against the SSRF guard, serves
  only bitmap content types, caps bodies at 8MB, and refuses third-party
  hotlinking. Previously it would echo attacker-controlled text/html back on
  the app's own origin.
- Third-party synopsis HTML is sanitized through a tag allowlist before
  rendering.
- trust proxy set, so rate limiting buckets per client rather than sharing
  one bucket behind Vercel's proxy.
- CORS declines unknown origins instead of throwing, which previously
  produced a 500 that bypassed the header middleware.
- Added a terminal error handler; six handlers no longer return raw driver
  messages.

Maintenance
- Sandbox reaper moved off a module-scope setInterval, which never fired on
  serverless, onto a secret-gated endpoint driven hourly by the workflow.
- Removed six unused dependencies including puppeteer and playwright, and
  regenerated package-lock.json so they are no longer installed for the
  lambda.
- ESLint config moved to the repo root; the previous script linted a single
  file and the whole src tree was never checked.

Show coach-facing sponsorship status, with a manual recheck

Exposes the sponsorship pipeline's output through the backend and into the
coach UI, without touching the pipeline itself: CSV parsing, register
finalization, candidate matching, the Claude resolver, RLS, and the crawler
are all unchanged.

Backend — GET/POST /sponsors/companies/{id}[/recheck]
--------------------------------------------------------
Upgraded the existing, unconsumed GET /sponsors/companies/{id} (previously raw
company_sponsorship_current rows + the latest check, no staleness handling) in
place, rather than adding a second, overlapping route — nothing in the
frontend called the old shape yet. Added POST .../recheck alongside it.

Both are coach-authenticated with plain `Depends(get_current_user)` — this
project has no coach/student role anywhere (no JWT claim, no profiles table:
confirmed by auditing app/ and the frontend's auth flow before writing any
code), and every existing coach-only route already uses exactly this as its
gate. That's the existing convention, not a new one invented for this
endpoint. The sponsorship tables stay service-role-only; the browser never
queries them directly, only the normalized status the backend computes.

Response is one of five states — licensed | ambiguous | no_match | error |
not_checked — never the raw table rows, and `error` never carries the
underlying exception text.

`licensed` reads from company_sponsorship joined to sponsor_licences directly
(not the `company_sponsorship_current` view, which lacks the
normalized_name/normalized_town needed for route grouping) and needs no
separate staleness check: it's current by construction, since finalization
keeps `sponsor_licences.is_current` live in real time and the natural-key
upsert keeps a licence row's id stable across editions. The other four states
come from company_sponsorship_checks, which DOES need one — checked against
`register_import_id` vs the latest successful import — because a check has no
independent freshness signal of its own. A stale check (including a stale
`match` decision whose licence is no longer current) reports `not_checked,
stale=true`, carrying the old check's own checked_at/candidate_count rather
than just going silent.

Multiple licence rows for one sponsor (one per route) are grouped by
(normalized_name, normalized_town) — the same identity key the candidate
matcher itself already uses, since the register carries no organisation-level
id — scoped to currently-listed rows only, so a card never shows a route the
organisation has since dropped.

Recheck reuses worker.resolve_companies(force=True, one company), not
service.resolve_company: the worker is the only path that writes
company_sponsorship_checks as well as company_sponsorship, so reusing the
one-shot resolver instead would leave the check row stale for an
ambiguous/no_match outcome. No matching logic is duplicated.

Frontend
--------
No coach-only company detail page exists in this app today — the coach
companies list links out to the PUBLIC /companies/[slug] page, which must
never carry sponsorship data. The closest fit, and the only coach-scoped
per-company route in the app, is the outreach composer
(/coach/outreach/[companyId]); the Sponsorship card sits there, next to
CompanyContextCard.

lib/sponsorship.ts fetches server-side on page load (mirrors getCompanyContext
— createSupabaseServerClient → getSession → fetch with a Bearer token) and
never throws: a missing session, a network failure, or a non-2xx response all
resolve to `null`, which the card renders identically to a genuine backend
`error` status ("Check unavailable", no raw error text). lib/sponsorship-api.ts
is the browser-side counterpart for the Recheck button, mirroring
outreach-api.ts/email-api.ts.

Product wording follows the brief: "No confirmed sponsor licence found" (never
"does not sponsor"), the disclaimer under a licensed result ("A sponsor
licence does not guarantee sponsorship for a specific vacancy"), ambiguous
shows candidate_count without presenting any one candidate as confirmed.

Tests
-----
test_sponsor_status_endpoint.py: A-G and J from the brief against a fake
database (licensed, route aggregation across current AND withdrawn siblings,
ambiguous, no_match, error-without-leaking-raw-text, not_checked, stale
detection including a stale match decision, confidence passthrough), plus H/I
through a real TestClient — authenticated reaches the handler, unauthenticated
is rejected. That rejection is 401, not 403: this codebase has no role that
would produce a 403, and manufacturing one here would be exactly the kind of
endpoint-specific behavior this milestone was told not to invent.

No frontend test runner or component-test convention exists anywhere in
apps/web (no vitest/jest, no .test.tsx files) — skipped per the brief's own
conditional rather than introducing one for this milestone. Verified instead
with `tsc --noEmit`, `eslint`, and a full `next build`, all clean.

Refresh JWTs could authenticate bearer routes, account activation could return selected password hashes, and pending TOTP seeds could complete temporary login. This patch closes those paths and applies the approved public-response, password, MFA-role, CSV, audit-IP and RSVP-deletion boundaries.

## Changes

- **S1/S3:** allowlist public comment authors and current-user profiles; preserve editable profile fields and populated roles, including blank-name roles with a slug fallback.
- **S2/S5:** require explicit access-token purpose on all three bearer paths; separate pending TOTP enrollment from enabled-factor login while retaining authenticated confirmation of legacy pending seeds.
- **S4:** share the 12-Unicode-character / 72-UTF-8-byte enrollment policy between server and registration/invitation, reset and guest-upgrade forms; add English/French guidance and correct the advisory meter. Existing-password sign-in remains compatible.

- **S8/S10:** use shared formula-safe CSV text encoding and validated Express `req.ip` under existing proxy trust.
- **S9:** self/admin account deletion cancels current/future RSVPs using the existing calendar UTC-day window, including ongoing/today events regardless of status, RSVP toggle or deadline. Preserve staff-only historical snapshots. Use idempotent cancellation audits, a post-deletion sweep and an account recheck to close in-flight RSVP writes. No cancellation emails, waitlist or capacity-counter behavior is introduced.
- **S7:** document the accepted public-bucket policy; random URLs are not access control. No bucket access or storage changes.

- Normal, unchanged `npm test`: **895 passed** (546 unit, 3 contract, 246 integration), zero failures/skips, using Node 24.19.0, npm 11.21.0 and isolated MongoDB 8.2.6.

- Independent source review caught and resolved blank-role response compatibility and the in-flight RSVP race; final re-review found no further actionable issue.
- Syntax, lint, OpenAPI parsing, `git diff --check`, and production static-asset packaging passed. Browser form handlers were tested in VM; no live-browser/VPS or production-data tests were performed.

## Rollout and remaining work

- No new environment variables, indexes, data migrations, dependency changes or bulk session revocation. Deploy all app instances together rather than mixing old/new token issuance and TOTP enrollment versions.
- Existing refresh cookies remain valid. Shared clients refresh/retry old untyped access tokens after 401; users without a valid refresh cookie must sign in again.
- **S6 follow-up:** fresh actor MFA confirmation and target-session revocation during reset are not implemented. This PR implements only the approved role boundary.
- Private uploads remain future work. Historical RSVP contacts remain staff-only; authored public text and public-bucket uploads are not automatically scrubbed by account deletion.

Fix critical auth vulnerabilities and make SOS dispatch fault-tolerant

SECURITY
Rotated the JWT signing secret, which was committed to the repo in
socket-server/test-sos.js and matched the live value in both .env files —
anyone with repo access could mint an ADMIN token. Removed that script and
get-users.js, plus the unauthenticated /api/test-email open mail relay and the
/debug-token page that rendered a live session token on screen.

Socket authentication took `role` from the client payload, so any user could
join the admin room and read every SOS alert's live GPS. Role and identity now
come from a DB lookup keyed on the verified token. All six SOS socket handlers
had no authorization at all: any authenticated user could resolve a live
emergency and tell the victim help had arrived. Each handler now derives
identity from socket.data and checks role.

Sessions are authoritative again — getUserFromToken consults the session row
and rechecks account status, so logout, password reset and suspension actually
revoke access instead of leaving a token live for 7 days. Session and reset
tokens are stored as SHA-256 digests.

Also: removed the hardcoded DB password and JWT fallback from socket-server;
fixed X-Forwarded-For spoofing that bypassed every rate limit; restricted file
uploads by MIME/extension/size (an .html upload into public/ was stored XSS);
added a default-deny proxy.ts gate over all 36 API routes; extracted
requireAdmin to replace 16 duplicated checks; unified the password policy;
HTML-escaped email templates; added CSP; upgraded Next 16.2.6 -> 16.2.12,
nodemailer -> 9.0.3, and pinned postcss/sharp.

SOS DISPATCH
POST /api/sos saved an alert and replied "Help is on the way" while
dispatching to nobody — the chain only ran on the WebSocket path. It now
triggers dispatch via an internal endpoint, and says so honestly when it
cannot.

Replaced the serial dispatch chain (one vendor at a time, 30s each, ~70s
before anyone real was asked) with parallel fan-out per severity tier, a
bounded search radius, and reliability-weighted vendor ranking. Accepts are
claimed with an atomic conditional UPDATE, so exactly one vendor wins even
across instances. Running out of vendors now escalates and pages on call
instead of leaving the caller on "Searching..." forever.

Added: caller location streaming, non-blocking GPS with IP fallback, duplicate
alert merging, location-verified arrival, caller-confirmed resolution, cancel
flow, caller-offline escalation, and a SosDispatchLog audit trail.

VERIFICATION
Both projects typecheck and build. security.check.ts covers the proxy
allowlist, token hashing, password policy, IP handling and upload rules.
dispatch.e2e.ts drives a real SOS through live sockets and a live database —
22/22 checks pass, confirming parallel pings (7ms spread vs ~20s serial),
radius exclusion, single-winner races, arrival rejection at distance, and

NOT DONE

fix(preference-cards): secure rebuild provenance writes

An independent review found the highest-priority claim of this branch to be
false. rebuild_provenance was described as writable only by the reviewed rebuild,
and it was not: authenticated holds INSERT on ip_user_preference_cards, the live
insert policy checked only user_id = auth.uid(), and the pending migration added
nothing but a before-update trigger. A signed-in user could POST straight to
PostgREST with their own user_id and an arbitrary JSON object in the column, and
the write-once trigger would then have frozen the forgery into something
indistinguishable from immutable reviewed evidence. Immutability is not
authenticity, and only the second one was worth anything here.

Three layers now stand between a caller and a provenance-bearing row. The
authenticated insert policy is replaced so an ordinary caller may insert only
rows whose provenance is null, which leaves ordinary card creation untouched
because saveUserCard never names the column. A before-insert trigger rejects a
non-null provenance from every role except one, which is what covers service_role
— it has bypassrls, so no policy can constrain it, and possessing a key is not
evidence that a review happened. And the only role the trigger trusts is
ip_preference_card_rebuild_writer, a nologin role that exists to own one function.

public.ip_create_rebuilt_preference_card is that function: security definer, empty
search path, execute revoked from public, anon and authenticated and granted only
to service_role. It is deliberately not a general card-insert endpoint. It always
writes status draft, never accepts a share token, leaves id, token, sharing and
timestamps to column defaults, and re-derives from the database every source fact
it can rather than trusting the payload for it — that the revision exists, belongs
to the named card, belongs to the named owner, and still carries the hashes and
release the provenance claims. The recheck and the insert are one statement, which
is what closes the validation-to-insert race: there is no window between the source
being verified and the row being written for a concurrent delete to land in.

The application keeps the authority split that makes any of this worth having.
Every owner-scoped read stays on the authenticated cookie client under row-level
security; only the final write uses rebuild-writer.server.ts, which carries
import 'server-only', exports one function, and deliberately does not re-export a
general admin client. Swapping a service client in for the reads would have turned
an owner-scoped feature into an unscoped one to solve a write problem.

The migration is also strict first-use DDL now — add column, add constraint,
create function, create trigger, with no if-not-exists and no or-replace on
anything it owns. It has never been applied, a failed transactional migration
rolls back cleanly, and tolerance only hides drift at the one moment drift is
worth discovering.

The verifier is rewritten because the old one could pass while all of this was
broken: it inserted both synthetic cards as postgres, so it never met row-level
security or the insert policy at all, and every negative case was caught with
exception when others, so any error counted as the expected one. It now runs as
authenticated and as service_role with real JWT context, asserts current_user
before each operation, names the exact SQLSTATE it expects and re-raises anything
else, exercises the trusted RPC including its source recheck and an owner
mismatch, proves all three write-once directions, proves rename, share and status
updates leave provenance alone, deletes its synthetic rows explicitly, and
compares exact counts and content digests against the baseline before rolling
back. Run it against a scratch schema whose policy omits the provenance condition
and Part 3 must fail; a verifier that cannot fail is not evidence.

The jest fake models roles for the same reason. It accepted the forged insert
before, which is why no test caught the blocker.

* chore: point everything at ap-south-1, since ap-southeast-1 is going away

The ap-southeast-1 project is being deleted, so every reference to it in
the repo is now wrong. Most are defaults and documentation. One is a
safety guard, and it is the reason this is worth doing carefully.

`e2e/seed-e2e.mjs` refuses to run when its target URL contains the
production ref, because that seeder "deletes and rewrites freely". The ref
it names is the old project. Left alone, the guard would protect a
database that no longer exists while the destructive seeders pointed
happily at the live one — a guard that has quietly stopped guarding is
worse than no guard, because nobody rechecks it. Twelve more e2e scripts
carry the same ref as a fallback URL, so an unset `SUPABASE_URL` sent them
to the old project; now it sends them to the current one, which is exactly
why the guard has to move with them.

`apps/mobile/eas.json` also carried the old anon key, so every EAS build
authenticated against the retired project. It now carries the ap-south-1
publishable key.

The baseline migration keeps the old ref on purpose. It is applied on
every database and editing it would change a checksum Prisma has already
recorded; the trigger that contained it was superseded earlier today by
one that reads its host from the vault, so nothing reads that literal any
more.

Two halves stay outside the repo and remain yours: `apps/mobile/.env` and
the Vercel environment on the web and admin projects.

* chore(ci): let the secret scan tell Supabase's two key formats apart

The scan failed on this branch, and it was right to look: `generic-api-key`
matched the key added to `eas.json`. It is the wrong verdict, though.

Supabase issues two formats. `sb_publishable_…` replaces the anon key — it
is compiled into every mobile binary and served in every web page, carries
no privilege of its own, and RLS is what actually guards the data behind
it. The file already held the JWT anon key it supersedes; that one simply
never matched the rule. Nothing became public here that was not public
before.

`sb_secret_…` is the service-role credential and bypasses RLS entirely, so
the allowlist matches the publishable prefix only. Widening it to `sb_`
would be the mistake, and is called out in the file so the next person
does not make it.

Verified against gitleaks 8.30.1 rather than assumed: `eas.json` scans
clean, a file containing an `sb_secret_` key still reports a leak, and the
branch's commit range is clean.

feat(settings-engine): Wave 1-3 — super_admin role + read/write API + test actions

Lets non-technical school admins self-serve operational config (SMTP, S3,
OIDC, Anthropic API key, etc.) that previously required editing .env and
restarting. Demo-to-pilot conversion becomes point-and-click instead of
shell-and-engineer.

WAVE 1 — foundation
─────────────────────
- Migration 000057 settings table (scope/key/value_plain/value_encrypted/
  value_type + 4 CHECK constraints + UNIQUE(scope, scope_id, key))
- Migration 000058 widens users.role CHECK to include 'super_admin'
- Setting GORM model with BeforeCreate defaults
- settings.Service with Get/GetEffective/Set/Clear; resolution order:
  user → account-parent-chain → instance → env → default. Secrets pass
  through auth.secretbox before storage; audit_log fires on every
  set/clear with no value in payload (incl. for non-secrets)
- 22-entry catalog covers SMTP/S3/Anthropic/SAML/OIDC/passkeys/branding/
  quotas. JWT_SECRET, MFA_ENCRYPTION_KEY, DATABASE_URL, ENVIRONMENT,
  FRONTEND_URL deliberately excluded (chicken-and-egg with the store
  that holds them).
- RequireSuperAdmin middleware + Protected/JWT path special-cases the
  role for cross-tenant access. Setup wizard promotes the first user to
  super_admin (was 'admin').

WAVE 2 — read API + Canvas-CVE-class hardening
────────────────────────────────────────────────
- GET /api/v1/superadmin/settings (list, secrets masked)
- GET /api/v1/superadmin/settings/:key (single, secrets masked)
- GET /api/v1/superadmin/settings/groups (catalog vocabulary, no live
  values — separate response shape so a UI bug can't unmask via
  debug serialization)
- Mounted via registerSuperAdminRoutes — the ONLY authorized place to
  attach /superadmin/* routes, structural protection against forgetting
  RequireSuperAdmin on a new endpoint
- Wave 2 audit (Canvas-LMS site_admin CVE precedent):
  - M3: dropped JWT-claim-derived is_super_admin Locals. Demoted
    super_admin used to retain cross-tenant powers via assertSameTenant
    for up to 24h (JWT TTL). Only DB-rechecking writers may now set
    the Locals; regression test in middleware/auth_test.go.
  - M1: setup wizard now wraps CompleteSetup in pg_advisory_lock to
    serialize across pods. Previously a 3-pod deployment hit
    concurrently could mint three super_admins.

WAVE 3 — write API + test actions + SSRF defense
──────────────────────────────────────────────────
- PUT/DELETE /api/v1/superadmin/settings/:key — write/clear with
  account-existence validation
- POST /api/v1/superadmin/settings/test/{email,oidc,anthropic,s3} —
  exercise current effective config against external dependencies
  for fast operator feedback
- Per-action rate limit (1/30s per (super_admin, action)) — distinct
  test endpoints don't share buckets, so operators can chain
  email→oidc→anthropic without delay but can't loop-test
- Threat model: super_admin authority is the deployment's settings,
  NOT its network position. Each test action explicitly bounded:
  - email: sends to caller's own email only (not body-controlled);
    no open-relay vector
  - oidc: SSRF guard (https-only, port 443, public-unicast IPs only,
    7 blocked hostname suffixes incl. .internal/.local, no redirects
    via CheckRedirect=http.ErrUseLastResponse)
  - anthropic: endpoint is a const (api.anthropic.com hard-coded);
    no body param can redirect the API key; also refuses redirects
  - s3: object key is paper-lms-settings-test/<crypto-rand-hex>.txt;
    body params named "key"/"object"/"path" are ignored
- Wave 3 audit fixes (post-shipping checklist):
  - C1 CRITICAL: OIDC discovery test followed 3xx redirects without
    re-running validateExternalURL — attacker.com → 302 → 169.254.169.254
    bypassed the SSRF guard entirely. Fixed with CheckRedirect override
    on both OIDC and Anthropic clients.
  - H2 HIGH: Clear handler defaulted to scope=instance on missing
    body. Destructive endpoint → now requires explicit scope (400).
  - M3/M4: test-action audit row now carries IP, User-Agent, and
    admin_account_id (or account_id) for forensic filterability.

TEST COVERAGE
─────────────
- 24 settings.Service unit cases (resolution chain at every scope
  combination, secret encrypt/decrypt round-trip, audit emission,
  cycle-safe parent walk)
- 13 super_admin role-gate cases including Canvas-CVE-class regressions
  (root-account admin must NOT inherit super-admin; near-miss role
  strings like "Super_Admin" must reject)
- 10 read-API handler cases (masking, source resolution, vocabulary
  shape, parent-chain hint, garbage input handling)
- 26 write-API + test-action cases (account-existence guard, scope

- M3 regression test locks "JWT-claim does not set is_super_admin
  Locals" — failure mode that would re-introduce the cross-tenant
  bypass

OUT OF SCOPE (next waves)
──────────────────────────
- Wave 4: React frontend panel at /superadmin/settings
- Wave 5: refactor env-var consumers (SMTPSender, S3StorageBackend,
  AIAssistService, OIDCHandler, PasskeyEngine, SAMLHandler) to read

  depth; super-admin-only attacker model makes this acceptable for v1)

commit.message:
Rebuild platform on Next.js + FastAPI/SQLAlchemy + Supabase Postgres

Full architectural rewrite per updated requirements: replaces the SQLite
MVP (moved to legacy/, frozen for reference) with a monorepo aimed at
long-term development — apps/api (backend), apps/web (dashboard),
services/ai (AI module scaffold).

apps/api (FastAPI + SQLAlchemy + Alembic):
- Schema: stocks, price_history, technical_indicators (precomputed
  cache, recomputed in full per sync — not patched incrementally),
  realtime_quotes, data_sync_log, stock_scores/ai_predictions (phase-2
  tables), watchlists/watchlist_items. UNIQUE constraints + upsert
  everywhere for no-duplicate guarantee; composite (stock_id, date DESC)
  indexes for time-series queries.
- Alembic configured for Supabase: excludes Supabase-managed schemas
  (auth/storage/realtime/...) from autogenerate diffing, uses DIRECT_URL
  (not the pooled connection) for migrations, shadow-tables auth.users

* Port the schema off Supabase: platform.sql

The first half of moving the database to DigitalOcean. supabase/schema.sql
protects four tables with row-level security and every one of its 18 guards
asks auth.uid(). On Supabase that function, auth.users, storage.objects and the
anon/authenticated roles came with the platform; on a plain PostgreSQL cluster
none of it exists and the app schema will not even load.

server/sql/platform.sql creates those objects for real, shaped so that
supabase/schema.sql applies on top UNCHANGED — same function name, signature
and semantics, same role names. Verified: platform.sql then schema.sql both
apply clean to an empty database, and all of test/verify_schema_behaviour.js
passes against the result.

That is the point of the whole design. The alternative — reimplementing
authorisation in the API service — would replace a model with 21 passing
adversarial checks with new untested code that decides who may approve a
payment. Instead the API will open a transaction, SET LOCAL ROLE and
SET LOCAL request.jwt.claim.sub to a uid it has verified, and let the database
enforce exactly what it enforces today.

WHAT PLATFORM.SQL ADDS
  * anon / authenticated / service_role, all NOLOGIN — nothing connects as
    them; the service switches with SET LOCAL ROLE, so a leaked database
    password is not also a leaked customer session.
  * auth.users with the columns Supabase kept private: encrypted_password,
    email_confirmed_at, recovery_token. No grant is issued on it, so a customer
    cannot read another customer's password hash through the same connection.
  * users_email_uniq on lower(email) — one address, one account.
  * auth.uid(), reading request.jwt.claim.sub with current_setting(..., true)
    so an anonymous request has no uid instead of raising.
  * storage.buckets/objects carrying the bytes in a `data` column, so
    schema.sql's proofs_insert_own / proofs_read_own_or_admin policies apply
    unchanged and a customer's bank slip is under the same RLS as its metadata
    rather than on a guessable URL in a second system.
  * auth.refresh_tokens, so logout can mean something server-side rather than
    only clearing localStorage.

* Keep the service worker out of /api

Moving the API onto the app's own origin made it visible to the service worker
for the first time, and the worker was about to cache it.

The guard reads:

    if (e.request.method !== "GET" || url.origin !== location.origin) return;

cross-origin, so that line ignored all of them. A same-origin /api/... GET
falls through instead to the network-first branch at the bottom of the handler,
whose failure path answers from the shell cache — so a momentary outage could
serve a CACHED profile, and on a studio phone that several people use, that is
one customer's account answering for another.

Nothing under /api is now cached, replayed or intercepted.

the base URL changed: a recheck stopped re-reading the profile, an armed retry
stopped clearing the wall, and a reconnect issued no profile read at all. I
first assumed the Playwright route glob had stopped matching, and measured that
instead of trusting it — "**/api/**" intercepts correctly. Running the same
suite against the previous commit in a separate worktree showed all three
passing there, which placed the fault in my change rather than in the tests.

The bug was in a file this migration had not touched. Nothing about the service
is wrong; what changed is where the requests go, and a cache that had never
been able to see them suddenly could.

* The migration runbook, and the two things that do not come across

Documents what only the owner can do — deploy the app, set JWT_SECRET, apply

PASSWORDS CANNOT BE MIGRATED. Supabase stores bcrypt; this service stores
scrypt, and a bcrypt hash simply never verifies. That is not a setting to flip:
supporting both would mean hand-rolling a bcrypt verifier, which is not a thing
to hand-roll in the file that decides whether a password is correct. Every
account has to set a new one. With a single account that is one signup; with
customers it is a reset for each, which needs SMTP working first.

is set, recover() still answers 200 — it must not reveal which addresses exist —
and no mail is sent, so a locked-out customer needs their password changed by
hand. Said in the runbook rather than discovered later.

COST IS NOT A WIN, and the runbook says so. A managed database plus a service
instance is comparable to or more than Supabase Pro, with more moving parts.
What it buys is one account, one bill, and nothing pausing itself after a week
idle. The prices are not quoted, because they change and a stale number in a

Implement password reset and OTP resend; map the remaining error codes

/auth/forgot-password, /auth/reset-password and /auth/resend-otp were one-line
stubs returning success unconditionally — no email sent, no password changed —
while emailService.js already held complete bilingual reset templates and
auth.js imported sendResetPasswordEmail without ever calling it. This was a
built feature left unwired, which is why it would pass a QA click-through.

My own earlier commit made it worse: those routes previously returned bare
English, and giving them codes turned the lie into a polished localized one in
two languages. A locked-out user was told a reset link was on its way.

Implementation reuses what already existed: resetPasswordToken and
resetPasswordExpires were already on the User model, and passwordResetAt was
already read by the login route to skip OTP for 24h but written by nothing.

- The reset token is stored as a SHA-256 hash and only the raw value is
  emailed, so a database leak yields no usable links. Single-use, 1-hour
  expiry matching what the email copy promises.
- New passwords are hashed with bcrypt explicitly — there is no pre-save hook
  on User, so assigning plaintext would have stored it in the clear. A test
  now fails if that hook ever appears, since the route would need rechecking.
- forgot-password and resend-otp return an identical response whether or not
  the account exists, and swallow email failures, so neither becomes an
  account-enumeration oracle. reset-password uses one code for "unknown token"
  and "expired" alike.
- Both email-sending routes now sit behind a dedicated limiter keyed on the
  target address, so one victim cannot be mail-bombed and burning that budget
  no longer blocks legitimate logins from the same IP.

Session revocation: a stateless 7-day JWT meant a password reset left an
attacker's existing token working for the rest of the week. User gains
tokensValidFrom; the reset sets it; the auth middleware rejects any token
whose iat predates it. This costs no extra query — getPrincipalState widens
the projection the disabled-check already reads behind its 30s cache, and the
route calls invalidatePrincipal so revocation is immediate. UserContext treats
the resulting SESSION_REVOKED as terminal, like ACCOUNT_DISABLED.

Also maps the 5 codes that reached the UI unmapped (ALREADY_SUBSCRIBED,
INSUFFICIENT_ROLE, ORG_CREATING, PLAN_CHECK_ERROR, USER_NOT_FOUND) plus 4 that
were handled by hand-rolled chains, so Hero and Profile now resolve through
the shared mapper. Every one of the 66 backend codes is now mapped.

feat(db): Migration 2 — dogs (owner-side foundation) (#4)

## Summary

Adds the first child table of profiles: `dogs`, many per owner. This is
also the first user-managed table — rows are created on demand by app
code (vs `profiles`, which is trigger-created from `auth.users` on
signup). The pattern established here will extend to most subsequent
tables in Phase 1.

## Schema

- `id` (uuid, gen_random_uuid)
- `owner_id` FK → `profiles` RESTRICT
- `name` NOT NULL, `breed`, `date_of_birth` (with CHECK rejecting future
dates), `temperament_notes`, `photo_url`
- `created_at` / `updated_at` / `deleted_at`
- `idx_dogs_owner_id` covers the only V1 query pattern ("this owner's
dogs"); composite `(owner_id, deleted_at)` deferred until profiling
shows it matters
- V1 deliberately omits `sex_at_birth` and `weight_lbs` — likely to come
up early given the working-dog community focus (PSA / Schutzhund /
French Ring trainers care about both for training selection); add via
column-add migration when first asked

## Why owner_id RESTRICT (not CASCADE)

Dogs are referenced by future bookings; losing them corrupts booking
history. Production user-deletion is anonymization (Phase 13), which
sets `deleted_at` and never triggers RESTRICT. RESTRICT is the safety
net for the unexpected hard-delete path — Postgres refuses loudly
instead of silently nuking history.

## RLS

Scope is owner-only for V1. The full Phase 1 spec also requires
"trainers see dogs of owners they have bookings with (including
completed/cancelled)." That requires a join against `bookings`, which
doesn't exist until Migration 6 — the trainer-read policy is added
there. No use case in Phases 3 / 4 / 5 needs trainer-read-dogs, so the
gap is invisible to users. Same forward-fix discipline as Migration 1b.

Three policies, all owner-scoped:

- **SELECT**: owners read their own dogs. Does NOT filter `deleted_at` —
booking-history joins need to find soft-deleted dogs that bookings
referenced; app code filters per query intent.
- **INSERT**: requires `auth.uid() = owner_id` AND user is
`role='owner'`, enforced via the EXISTS-subquery role-check pattern from
`database-agent.md`. Defense in depth on top of UI/route gating —
trainers cannot add dogs even by accident.
- **UPDATE**: owners update their own. No role recheck — dogs created
when role was verified are still THEIR records even if a Phase-12 admin
later promotes the user to trainer.
- No DELETE policy AND no DELETE grant — soft-delete only, two layers
refusing the operation.

## GRANTs

`SELECT` / `INSERT` / `UPDATE` to `authenticated`. No anon grants — dogs
are never publicly visible. This is the first table where "anon needs
nothing" is the right answer. Pattern going forward: ask "does anon
legitimately need this table?" Yes → grant + policy. No → no grant.
Rejecting at the GRANT layer is cheaper, earlier, and more explicit than
rejecting at the RLS layer.

## Verified

End-to-end against remote dev (`iomaiasjqozunjbvsdsk`):

- Schema, 3 policies, trigger, index all present in Studio
- Phase B: insert as owner-test (impersonated via JWT) succeeded; row
visible via service-role select
- Phase C — RLS proven across four sub-tests:

| Sub-test | Action | Result | What it proves |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | SELECT as owner-test | 1 row | Policy 1 matches | | C2 | SELECT
as trainer-test | 0 rows | No policy matches non-owner | | C3 | SELECT
as anon | ERROR 42501 at GRANT layer | No anon grant — Layer 1 rejection
| | C4 | INSERT as trainer-test | ERROR 42501 RLS policy violation |
role-EXISTS subquery rejects — Layer 2 rejection |

C3 vs C4 demonstrates the two-layer model cleanly: anon hits the GRANT
wall before RLS even runs, while authenticated trainer with INSERT grant
gets through to RLS and is rejected by the policy.

- \`supabase/migrations/20260506030637_dogs.sql\` (new)
- \`types/supabase.ts\` (regenerated, +47 lines)

docs(pipelines): amend pipeline 00001 auth boundary and id format (#5)

Amends pipeline 00001's spec. It changes D2, the auth boundary, and adds
D6, the id format. Nothing in 00001 is built yet, and its intent is
unchanged.

## D2 — Auth owns organizations; API checks them on every request

D2 is now binding on every pipeline that adds an organization-scoped API
action, a table whose rows belong to an organization, or a foreign key
into `auth`. A later pipeline breaks it by acting before the per-request
check, by leaving an organization's table without a foreign key to it,
or by making a foreign key to an organization cascade.

- Auth owns organizations, members, roles, and invitations, through
Better Auth's organization plugin. An organization is what the intent
calls a workspace. The business schema no longer holds membership rows.
- A token carries only `sub` and the standard claims. The `owner_sub`
claim is gone, and no organization, role, or permission is in the token.
The prefix of `sub` says whether the caller is a user (`usr_`) or an API
key (`key_`).
- Each request names its organization. Better Auth's active organization
is not used, and Auth keeps it empty through a session hook, so a call
to Better Auth that names no organization never acts on the one the user
last created or joined.
- API checks the caller on every request, and answers a failure in one
of three ways:
- **Unauthorized:** `sub` is missing or malformed, or the key is
deleted, disabled, or expired.
- **Not found:** the caller is not in the organization, or it does not
exist.
- **Forbidden:** the caller is in the organization, but its role or the
key's permissions do not allow the action.
- An API key belongs to its organization, not to the member who created
it, and Auth configures the key plugin with `references:
"organization"`. Removing that member leaves the key working, and
nothing records who created it. This reverses the old rule that removing
a creator blocks their credentials.
- Removing a member, changing a role, revoking a key, or changing a
key's permissions takes effect on the next request. An issued session
token outlives its revoked session by up to 15 minutes. That is the cost
of API verifying tokens without calling Auth or reading its sessions.
The membership check still applies to the token.
- Joining an organization needs a verified email. Auth sets Better
Auth's `requireEmailVerificationOnInvitation` to `true` explicitly,
because D6's id generator would otherwise switch it on silently. A team
deployment needs email delivery before a teammate can join. A single
operator does not.
- Organization deletion is off, through Better Auth's
`disableOrganizationDeletion`. Better Auth's delete would leave the
organization's API keys behind, and business rows would block it. A
pipeline that needs deletion defines one lifecycle for both.
- API's tables live in a `pipewhere` schema, with foreign keys to
organizations in `auth`. A privileged setup step creates both schemas
and roles. Auth's migrations run before API's.
- Auth grants API's database role read access column by column, plus
references to organization ids. API cannot read session tokens, password
hashes, or sign-in providers' tokens. Auth's role has no access to
`pipewhere`. Worker connects as API's role.
- A foreign key to an organization never cascades, and backs up deletion
being off. A row that records which API key acted keeps the key's id
with no foreign key, so it survives Better Auth deleting the key.
- API's tests run against Auth's real tables, and rerun when Auth's
migrations or Better Auth's version change.
- The overturn list names only the conditions that would change D2, not
replacement designs.

## D6 — Every id is a short prefix and a UUIDv7

- An id looks like `usr_01m36mep00e3ca12pwd1gkjwex`: a prefix of 3 to 5
letters, then a UUIDv7 as 26 lowercase base32 characters. It is at most
32 characters. This is the TypeID format.
- It binds every pipeline that adds a table with its own id, including
Auth's tables.
- Pipewhere's tables check the format with a constraint. Better Auth's
tables do not, so Auth never alters a table Better Auth migrates. Auth's
id generator throws for a table with no listed prefix.
- A prefix is never reused. Once the id generators exist, one test reads
both Auth's and API's mappings and checks it.

## Evidence

The spec's evidence section records:

- Better Auth's source at `3d0efa3`, dated 2026-09-22, as the source of
every statement about Better Auth in D2 and D6, plus three constraints
D2 does not state: the key-to-token exchange is Auth's own endpoint, key
permissions can be set only from server code, and Auth must define the
JWT payload. Auth pins no version yet, so the build rechecks these.
- A throwaway PostgreSQL 18 container: column grants, foreign keys
needing only `REFERENCES`, and a plain foreign key refusing the
referenced row's delete.

Nothing on D2's verification list has run. It needs Auth and API to
exist.

## Reviewer focus

- Team deployments now need email delivery, or a sign-in provider that
verifies email, before a teammate can join. A single operator is
unaffected.
- API keys have no foreign keys into `auth`. A later pipeline that adds
a row existing only for one key brings back the `REFERENCES` grant and a
cascading foreign key for it.
